title: Given two integers N and K, return all possible combinations of K numbers chosen from the range 1 to N. Explain the backtracking technique with a start index and how to prune when not enough numbers remain.
shortTitle: Combinations (All Ways to Choose K Items from N)

s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack choosing numbers in increasing order up to size K, and prune branches that cannot reach K items.
s1_definition.profdef:
Combinations enumerates every size-K subset of the numbers 1 through N.

- **Start value** ensures numbers are picked in strictly increasing order, so each combination appears once.
- **Base case** is when the current combination holds exactly K numbers, and a copy is recorded.
- **Pruning** stops branches where the remaining numbers are fewer than the slots still needed.
- **Result count** is N choose K, the binomial coefficient C(N, K).
- **Fixed-size specialization** makes this a restricted version of general subset generation.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a review committee must pick exactly 3 auditors from a pool of 6, and HR wants every possible committee. Order does not matter, so picking auditors 1 and 2 is the same committee as 2 and 1. They build committees by always choosing auditors in increasing number, so each committee is formed exactly once, and they stop early if too few auditors remain to fill the committee.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combinations enumerates every way to choose K numbers from the range 1 to N, where order does not matter. I solve it with backtracking using a start value and a current partial combination. When the combination reaches size K I record a copy. Otherwise I loop over numbers from the start onward, add one, recurse with the start advanced by one so picks strictly increase, and backtrack.

Choosing in strictly increasing order is exactly what distinguishes a combination from a permutation, because it fixes one canonical ordering per subset so no subset is produced twice. The optimization I always add is pruning: if the numbers still available are fewer than the slots I still need to fill, the branch cannot succeed, so I bound the loop end and avoid wasted work.

At National Bank of India I used this to enumerate audit committees, choosing exactly K auditors from a numbered pool of N so HR could run a conflict-of-interest review over every possible committee. I chose auditors in increasing order and pruned branches that could not be completed.

The result count is the binomial coefficient C(N, K), which can be computed directly without generating all combinations. For moderate N and K the enumeration is feasible, but for large N the output grows quickly, so I always check the count before generating.

Remember one sentence: pick numbers in increasing order up to size K, prune when not enough numbers remain, and the result count is C(N, K).

---

keyPoints: Combinations enumerates every size-K subset of the numbers 1 through N where order does not matter
A start value ensures numbers are picked in strictly increasing order, generating each combination once
Pruning stops branches where remaining numbers are fewer than the slots still needed to fill
The result count is the binomial coefficient C(N, K) = N! / (K! * (N-K)!)
This is the fixed-size specialization of general subset generation
Passing i + 1 on recursion ensures each number is used at most once per combination
The pruning bound is i <= N - (K - current.size()) + 1
